subject: maths
title: Decimals: numbers between whole numbers
intro: Not everything comes in whole numbers — money, heights, and measurements often fall between them. Decimals let us write those in-between amounts using the same place-value idea you already know, just extended past a dot. This lesson shows what the digits after the decimal point mean and how decimals connect to fractions.

sections.heading: Place value keeps going
body: You know that places to the left get ten times bigger: ones, tens, hundreds. Decimals extend the same pattern to the **right**, where each place gets ten times **smaller**. The **decimal point** marks where the whole numbers end. The first place after it is **tenths** (each a tenth of one), then **hundredths**, and so on.
So **0.3** means 3 tenths, which is the fraction 3/10. The bar below is split into ten equal parts with three shaded — that is 0.3 of the whole bar.

diagram.caption: 0.3 means 3 tenths — three of the ten equal parts.

sections.heading: Tenths, hundredths, and fractions
body: A decimal is really just a **fraction with a denominator of 10, 100, 1000…** written a shorter way. **0.7** is 7/10. **0.45** is 45/100. Reading two places after the point gives you hundredths, so 0.45 is forty-five hundredths — the same 45-out-of-100 idea as a percentage.

Some decimals equal familiar fractions: **0.5 = 1/2** (five tenths is a half), **0.25 = 1/4**, and **0.1 = 1/10**. Knowing these by heart helps you move between decimals, fractions and percentages easily.

diagram.caption: 0.45 means 45 hundredths — 45 of the hundred small squares.

sections.heading: Reading and comparing decimals
body: To compare decimals, line up the decimal points and compare digit by digit from the **left**, just like whole numbers. A common trap: **0.5 is bigger than 0.45**, even though 45 looks like a bigger number than 5 — because 0.5 is five tenths (0.50) while 0.45 is forty-five hundredths, and 50 hundredths is more than 45.
A safe trick is to give them the same number of decimal places by adding zeros: 0.5 becomes 0.50, and now 0.50 versus 0.45 is easy to compare. Money works exactly this way — $0.50 is more than $0.45.

steps: Give them the same number of places: 0.5 = 0.50.
Now compare 0.50 and 0.45 — like comparing 50 and 45 hundredths.

practice.q: What does the first digit after the decimal point show?
practice.explain: The first place after the point is tenths; the next is hundredths, each ten times smaller.
0.3 means 3 tenths, which is the fraction 3/10.
0.5 is five tenths, which is the same as one half (1/2).
Two places after the point are hundredths, so 0.45 is forty-five hundredths, 45/100.
Write 0.5 as 0.50; then 0.50 (fifty hundredths) is bigger than 0.45 (forty-five hundredths).

summary: Decimals extend place value to the right of the point: tenths, then hundredths, each ten times smaller.
A decimal is a fraction with denominator 10, 100…: 0.3 = 3/10, 0.45 = 45/100.
Compare by lining up points and matching decimal places (0.5 = 0.50 > 0.45).
